headline: New law adds protections and independence for the internal watchdog at the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
what_it_does: If GAO removes or transfers its Inspector General (the official who investigates problems inside GAO), it must give both chambers of Congress a written, detailed, case-specific reason at least 30 days in advance. Only the Comptroller General, who heads GAO, may place the Inspector General on non-duty status, and only under set rules. GAO must pass along the Inspector General's yearly budget request to Congress without changing it. The Inspector General must get legal advice from a lawyer who reports directly to the Inspector General or to another inspector general.

who_it_affects.how: Gains advance notice rules for removal or transfer, a budget request GAO cannot change, and their own legal counsel.

who_it_affects.group: GAO leadership, including the Comptroller General
who_it_affects.how: Must explain any removal or transfer of the Inspector General to Congress in writing 30 days ahead and follow limits on placing the Inspector General on non-duty status.
Receive written explanations before the Inspector General is removed or transferred, and see the Inspector General's budget request as written.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted November 25, 2024; the summary does not list a separate effective date.
